playbook:
When a new common-resource game starts, I compute the total sustainable extraction (stock × regrowth rate, split across players) and treat that as my default. A modest early grab above share is defensible only while the stock is full and regrowth is strong, and I cap it so the stock survives even if everyone grabs hard — but I should expect at least one player to defect from the start and not waste the opening being the only restrained boat.

My early-grab budget is one move, at most two, each smaller than the last. After that I reassess based on what others actually did, not on what I hoped they'd do — restraint is only worth continuing if the group shows signs of following it.

Unilateral conservation against a persistent defector does not work. In my last episode I took the sustainable share for four straight seasons while one boat kept taking 3–8× share, and the stock collapsed anyway — my restraint bought nothing and cost me everything. New rule: if after two seasons of my restraint the defector has not responded and the stock is still falling, I stop subsidizing his catch with my savings and take at least enough to claim my share of what's left before he drains it.

When I model the danger zone, I track the worst player's extraction rate, not the average. If one player consistently takes an amount that, combined with even moderate takes from others, exhausts the stock in N seasons, I plan for collapse at season N and make sure I've banked my share before then.

Matching the sustainable share is only my strategy when others match it too. The moment the data show someone defecting, the value of looking cooperative drops to near zero — the fishery ends in a race whether I join it or not, so I'd rather join it late than never.

In the endgame (final season, or any season where the stock will be dead before meaningful regrowth), I take as much as can be safely landed: roughly stock minus what I expect others to grab, computed so my submission cannot be zeroed out. In the last episode the stock hit 1.0 by the final season precisely because I conserved all game — the lesson is to arrive at the endgame with more stock remaining, which means defending my share mid-game, not arriving with less.

When the stock is low but not terminal and a defector is still active, I take my proportional share of the remaining stock rather than a fixed small number — this keeps pace with the race without being the one to kill the stock.

Every submission, I run the arithmetic: current stock, expected extraction by each other boat (using their observed pattern, not the cooperative ideal), regrowth of the remainder, and seasons left. I only under-take the sustainable share when the model shows the group as a whole is on a survivable path.

1.text:
On the opening season, when the stock is at its richest, I harvest hard — well above the sustainable share — because early fish are worth more than fish in any future season, and I cannot count on rivals to restrain themselves. But I never push so hard that a total strip by all boats collapses the stock in a single season; leave enough that even greedy rivals can't zero it.

I watch the revealed catches each season. If others are fishing above sustainable, I match that escalation immediately rather than fishing politely; holding back while rivals strip the stock only transfers future fish to them. Moderation is worthless as a unilateral signal.

I check who is actually doing the damage. In my last game the later seasons showed rivals had dropped to near-sustainable while my own large takes were driving the collapse. Matching escalation only makes sense while rivals are still escalating; once they back off, I can grab the dominant share without fear of a race, and I should size my take to keep the regrowth from being fully cancelled.

If a round of restraint does emerge — everyone drops to the sustainable share and the stock stabilizes — I still take above the share if I can do so without triggering re-escalation, because a stable low-stock fishery pays less than a slightly larger personal take that the stock can absorb.

With two or fewer seasons left, fractional fish are nearly worthless: regrowth can't rebuild the stock in time. I take a large share of what remains, enough that even if rivals grab hard there is still enough left for a meaningful final sweep.

On the final season, I abandon all conservation and submit for the entire remaining stock, not just my share — leftovers score nobody anything. I keep this habit regardless of how the season has gone.

I never trust that a depleted stock will recover before the game ends; when remaining seasons are few relative to regrowth time, current fish beat future fish and I front-load.

I verify each season that my submitted catch is what I intended before sending, and I track the running total so endgame takes are sized to beat, not tie, convenient round numbers.

2.text:
When the pool is large and regrowth is strong, I take above the sustainable share early — roughly 1.5–2× the stated share — because early fish are worth the most while the stock is high, but never so much that the fishery risks collapse if others are also aggressive. Early aggression paid off: most of my total came from the first two seasons.

When I see the season's total landings and the new stock figure, I identify each boat's behavior pattern, not just the average. If one boat is a persistent defector, I treat it as a fixed grabber in my forecasts rather than assuming it will ever cooperate.

This time proved the key lesson: restraint against a defector is a losing move. In seasons 4–5 I dropped to the sustainable share while boat 1 kept taking 8–9.5, and the stock crashed to 1.0 anyway — my restraint bought nothing, cost me points, and didn't save the fishery. So when one boat keeps over-harvesting regardless, unilateral sustainability is pointless: before switching to restraint, I check that my restraint can actually stabilize the stock. If stock minus (my sustainable take + the defector's expected take) still leaves the fishery collapsing, I take at least the defector's level to claim the fish before he destroys them, rather than letting the stock die while I'm being virtuous.

Only switch to sustainable-share harvesting when the arithmetic shows my restraint plus plausible others leaves the fishery viable — i.e., when all boats are near-sustainable or a stabilizer is identifiable and my share genuinely moves the outcome.

When the final season comes, I do not take the sustainable share. I note that there is no future to protect, and instead I take roughly my one-third split of the entire remaining stock (rounded slightly to be safe), since every fish left in the water at the end is worth zero. This time I took 0.3 of a 1.0 stock — the principle was right even though the defector had left almost nothing to claim. The mistake this game was not the ending; it was the seasons of cooperation that let the stock drain into his hands.

I never submit zero or a token amount once the fishery is alive, and I never take so much alone that my own catch could zero the stock before the final season unless my third of the remainder would exceed it.

I keep the arithmetic straight each season: post-catch stock = current stock minus total landings; next stock = 1.5 × that, capped at the maximum. I use this to test whether a planned over-harvest is survivable before submitting it, and to test whether my restraint would actually change the trajectory.
